page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E5.Flex.2-32 is a flexible virtual compute instance built on the x86_64 architecture. It is powered by the AMD EPYC 9J14 processor running at a base clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The instance configuration allocates 4 virtual CPUs derived from 2 dedicated physical cores with 2 threads per core. System memory is provisioned at 32.0 GB of RAM, yielding an elevated 1:8 vCPU-to-memory ratio.

The instance does not include integrated local storage, requiring network-attached storage volumes for persistent data and operating system installations. It features no hardware accelerators or GPUs. Dedicated CPU allocation ensures predictable single-tenant core behavior without thread contention from neighboring instances. Network connectivity includes 1 complimentary public IPv4 address.

With 8.0 GB of RAM per vCPU, this instance offers high memory density relative to its processing footprint. This balance allows cost-efficient resource utilization for deployments requiring substantial memory allocation without paying for excess compute cores. It fits workloads such as in-memory data stores, caching layers, relational database servers, ETL data processing, and memory-heavy enterprise backend services.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E5.Flex.2-32 is a memory-oriented virtual machine configured on the x86_64 architecture using AMD EPYC 9J14 processors running at 2.3 GHz. The instance provisions 4 vCPUs across 2 dedicated physical cores with multithreading, paired with 32.0 GB of system memory to maintain a high 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. Hardware acceleration is not present, and the instance includes no integrated local storage, depending entirely on network-attached storage solutions. One complimentary public IPv4 address is provided for network accessibility. By offering a sizable memory capacity alongside dedicated compute cores, this configuration provides a balanced resource distribution for workloads with substantial working memory requirements. It is well suited for in-memory caches, small-to-midsize relational databases, ETL processing, and memory-intensive enterprise application tiers that do not demand extensive CPU core counts.
